title: The Barred Doors of El Pedregal
story:
The path descending from the chalk ridge was steep and chalky, kicking up pale plumes of powder with every step James took. Below, the settlement sat nestled in the shadow of the basin like a dry bone caught between stones. There were no bright paper kites dancing in the sky here, no sweet smell of boiling maize drifting across the gullies, and no rhythmic clack of a carpenter's adze echoing from an open yard. It was a place called El Pedregal, built from sun-cracked adobe and slumped slate tiles, weathered down to the color of dry river silt.

James walked past cracked walls that offered no shade. He walked past bolted timber gates that offered no passage. He walked past hollow window grilles that offered no friendly eyes. When he reached the central dust lane, a woman carrying a bucket of washwater stopped dead in her tracks, glared at his leather strap and brass canisters with hard, guarded suspicion, and sharply jerked her chin toward the road. Down the alley, a shopkeeper swept gravel from a threshold, spotted James approaching, and clattered the heavy handle of his reed broom against the stone wall with a loud, ringing strike, yelling a harsh '¡Fuera!' that sent a stray dog scurrying into the shadows.

James pulled back, tucking his tail close against his flank. In Oakhaven there had been Barnaby's gentle apple slice; in San Gabriel there had been Don Tadeo's steady nod. But here, the eyes that watched him through cracked wooden shutters were pinched tight with fear or grievance, warning him that he did not belong. He did not offer his customary whispered greeting to the square. The air felt too sharp for it, smelling not of flowers or hearthfires, but of stale limestone and oncoming lightning.

By late afternoon, the southern horizon curdled into a bruised, menacing indigo. A violent highland gale swept over the ridge, howling through the narrow alleys and throwing grit against the barred doors until the entire village sealed itself into complete silence. Left alone in the swirling dirt as the first fat drops of rain struck the gravel like thrown pebbles, James scurried toward the settlement's rugged southern edge. There, half-swallowed by thorn bushes, stood a massive, sagging timber barn with a rusted corrugated roof. Slipping through a gap where the grey planks had rotted away, he huddled deep into a pile of dry, cobwebbed straw just as the heavens tore open in a deafening deluge.
